record.original_question: Start with the natural numbers and build the binary sieve by deleting every 2nd remaining number, then from what remains deleting every 4th remaining number, then every 2^k-th remaining number for each k = 1, 2, 3, .... Does the resulting sequence contain infinitely many primes, and also infinitely many composite numbers?

evidence.quote: Conjectures: - there are an infinity of primes that belong to this sequence; - there are an infinity of numbers of this sequence which are not prime.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Define a sequence of subsets $A_0 \supseteq A_1 \supseteq A_2 \supseteq \cdots$ of the positive integers as follows. Set $A_0 = \mathbb{N} = \{1,2,3,\dots\}$, written in increasing order. For each $k \ge 1$, obtain $A_k$ from $A_{k-1}$ by deleting every $2^k$-th term in the increasing enumeration of $A_{k-1}$; that is, at stage $k=1$ delete every 2nd remaining number, at stage $k=2$ delete every 4th remaining number, at stage $k=3$ delete every 8th remaining number, and so on. Let $S = \bigcap_{k\ge 0} A_k$ be the resulting "binary sieve" sequence of surviving integers.

Prove or disprove the following two statements:
(a) $S$ contains infinitely many prime numbers.
(b) $S$ contains infinitely many composite numbers.
artifact.status_search_result: The questions appear as conjectures in compilations of unsolved Smarandache-type sieve problems. No search result indicates a resolution; questions of this type (primes in sieve-defined thin sequences) are generally beyond current techniques due to the parity problem.
